title: Bezzecchi denies Marquez top spot in overshadowed practice
author: Eden Hannigan
text:
Marco Bezzecchi topped the first practice MotoGP session at Valencia that was overshadowed by Marc Marquez’s retirement announcement just before the day’s action started.

Marquez produced a pre-prepared slideshow on cards with a statement before the start of FP1, announcing that the Valencian Grand Prix will be his last weekend as a MotoGP rider.

The rest of the action on track paled in comparison to the talk off track, with the speculation increasing over Ducati's future line-up following the bombshell announcement.

However, Bezzecchi took matters into his own hands with the on-track action, as he set a 1m30.681s.

With Bezzecchi still hunting team-mate Aprilia Jorge Martin for second in the championship, he started off his weekend strongly at a track where he won in 2025.

Marquez was a close second, just 0.010 seconds off top spot amid the heavy attention on him after the breaking news.

Trackhouse Aprilia’s Raul Fernandez completed the top three ahead of Gresini Ducati pair Fermin Aldeguer and Alex Marquez.

Pedro Acosta - whose 2027 at Ducati now looks pretty different - was sixth, while Johann Zarco crashed towards the end of FP1 but still took seventh over Fabio Di Giannantonio.

Martin was ninth, 0.504s off team-mate Bezzecchi’s best time, as Ai Ogura completed the top 10.

title: Momentous decision looms after judges call for Netanyahu charges to be dropped
author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
text:
Dropping of corruption charges against PM after highly unusual intervention could set damaging precedent

The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

“There were evidentiary difficulties in the case, but the position the judges laid out effectively means abandoning the media to the whims of politicians and publishers, and setting an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases,” said Yael Freidson, the legal correspondent for Haaretz, who has covered the trial since it began in 2020.

The judges urged prosecutors to drop one case because “the chances of a conviction are low”, seek a plea deal in a second, and reconsider the third set of charges. Even if prosecutors were to prove the allegations of fraud and breach of trust in that case, it was not clear that Netanyahu’s alleged behaviour amounted to criminal conduct, they said.

The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, who was summoned to court to hear the judges’ statement in person, must now decide whether to accept their recommendations and end a trial that has dominated and shaped Israeli politics for the best part of a decade.

The decision is not straightforward, even though the current bench has in effect indicated a not guilty verdict is a foregone conclusion. If the trial continues, their ruling could still be appealed to a higher court, where fresh judges could take a different stance.

“[The former prime minister] Ehud Olmert was acquitted on all charges by the district court and was subsequently convicted by the supreme court on a minor charge,” Ben Caspit wrote in Maariv. “It ain’t over till it’s over.”

“[Baharav-Miara] could opt to reach a lenient plea bargain agreement with the defendant and put it all to rest, but that would be an admission of the entire justice system’s failure and would further fuel the conspiracy theories that Netanyahu and his disciples have been pumping ever since he was indicted.”

Settling or dropping all charges would immediately and permanently absolve Netanyahu, ending the threat of jail time and dispelling the legal shadow hanging over his political future.

A bill making its way through the opposition-controlled parliament would in effect bar him from serving as prime minister until the trial was concluded.

Netanyahu, who has pleaded not guilty to all charges, claims he is the victim of a political witch-hunt and welcomed the judges’ recommendation as a vindication. “The truth has finally come to light,” he said.

Baharav-Miara has withstood pressure from the judges in the case twice before. In 2023 and in 2025 they urged prosecutors to drop bribery charges, the most serious ones that Netanyahu faces, although they stopped short of suggesting the whole trial should be wrapped up.

Perhaps the single point of agreement between Netanyahu’s supporters and his critics in relation to the trial is concern that it has been allowed to drag on for too long. Testimony from Netanyahu had extended over a year and a half, across 98 hearings, the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history, Freidson said. The transcripts from all the hearings run to more than 60,000 pages.

Oren Persico has sat in every hearing since the case began in 2020, covering it for the investigative magazine The Seventh Eye. Over that period he watched the judges slowly lose control of their courtroom, he said.

“It started with giving the defence a lot of rope to do what they wanted. Netanyahu’s lawyer lashed out at the prosecution and humiliated them, almost every day, and attacked the judges, which should be an absolute red line in court,” he said. “I think the judges are afraid and tired; they just want to get it all over with.”

The sense of a bench cracking under pressure was exacerbated by the recommendation to reconsider charges in one of the cases against Netanyahu. These were laid out by prosecutors seven years ago, and have not changed since, prompting joking questions about whether the judges had even read the indictment, and serious ones about their political judgment.

When Netanyahu was indicted, he decided to fight the charges both inside and outside the courtroom, declaring war on the prosecution, the media, the police and key democratic and judicial institutions, Persico said.

“To keep himself out of jail, he tried to form an authoritarian state here in Israel, which tore apart society. I understand the interest in putting an end to that,” Persico said. “But ending the trial would send a terrible message to criminals and politicians and media bosses: that if you fight strongly enough you can get away with anything.”

title: ‘They Ran Out of Time’: Why Artem Shmidt Left Ineos for NSN
author: ahood
text:
Shmidt, a winner at the Classique Dunkerque in May, is heading to NSN. (Photo: Luc Claessen/Getty Images)

America might have its next cobblestone beast in Artem Shmidt .

The young American got his first real taste of the punishing cobbles in 2026, and it left him hungry for more .

And he’s already hooked on racing in Belgium.

“I don’t think there’s a greater feeling in the world than going up Kwaremont for the third time in a bike race with thousands of people screaming at you with those passionate Belgian fans,” Shmidt said this week. “That was a quite incredible feeling.”

With a move from Netcompany-Ineos to NSN Cycling for 2027, Shmidt is hoping to find the freedom to chase more results and develop his skills on the pavé .

No American man has ever hoisted the cobblestone trophy in the Paris-Roubaix velodrome or won the Tour of Flanders .

It’s way too early to pile that sort of pressure on his shoulders, but Shmidt packs a big engine coupled with strong time trialing chops that promise a lot more.

Shmidt’s transfer to NSN comes at an important crossroads in his career . Many say that the second contract to confirm a spot in the WorldTour is often the most challenging for a young pro.

After cutting his teeth in the WorldTour with two full seasons with Netcompany-Ineos, the Georgian penned a three-year deal with NSN.

The arrivals of Primož Roglič and Richard Carapaz grabbed the biggest headlines , but Shmidt fits into the younger more aggressive part of NSN’s recruitment class.

“The team reached out to me quite early, sometime in the spring, and I was pretty keen off the bat,” Shmidt said during a media call this week.

“By the time we got things figured out, it was probably around Tour time, I talked with Ineos out of respect for them. I wanted to let them know what was happening,” he said.

“I was talking to other teams, and you guys probably know that sometimes it takes a little bit long to get things done with Netcompany. They ran out of time, and I ended up signing NSN, which I’m super grateful for. I’m looking forward to it and can’t wait to get things started.”

At Netcompany, he was way down the pecking order. At NSN, he expects more freedom.

“I like to not have a leash on and just race aggressively,” Shmidt said.

Shmidt’s calendar for 2027 remains TBD, but he will keep building out his time trial skills and get another shot at the northern classics. Racing a grand tour is also on his wish-list.

At 6-foot-2 and 170lbs, some say he has a build like Fabian Cancellara or his ex-Ineos teammate Filippo Ganna. Everyone’s been telling him he’s made for the classics since he started racing as a junior.

“I really fell in love with the classics and growing up watching them,” he said. “Everyone kind of tells you already that you’re going to be a classics rider just based off my physique and everything. So I was already quite mentally prepared to be a classics rider and that racing style.”

Netcompany-Ineos gave him a full taste in 2026, from Omloop Het Nieuwsblad all the way through Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix. He was even thrown into Amstel Gold Race and La Flèche Wallonne.

There were no major results, but he came out the other side stronger and hungrier.

That cobblestone initiation in part led to his breakout first European pro win at the Classique Dunkerque in France in early May.

NSN took notice and was quick to chase his signature for the team’s 2027 rebuild.

“Artem Shmidt is one of the most exciting talents to come out of the U.S. in recent years,” said NSN manager Kjell Carlström. “A big objective for us is to continue facilitating that development and see just how far he can go in one-day and stage races.”

The American men’s peloton has produced Tour de France winners, world champions, and some of the best time trialists in the history of the sport, yet the cobblestone monuments remain elusive.

George Hincapie came close, finishing second at Paris-Roubaix in 2005 and third at the Tour of Flanders in 2006.

Tyler Hamilton’s victory at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2003 remains the lone American victory across any of the men’s five monuments.

Shmidt, 23 in January, seems destined to find his place in the northern classics.

He raced in Europe as a teenager and split his time as a junior between the Belgian Cannibal squad and the American Hot Tubes program before stepping up to the U23 ranks with Hagens Berman.

Netcompany-Ineos opened the door to the WorldTour as a stagiaire in 2024, and now NSN will give him even more freedom in his deal through 2029.

“My goal [at Ineos] was just to learn as much as possible, and now hopefully at NSN I can try to become the best version of myself,” he said. “I won in Dunkirk with the late attack. I like to race aggressively, not overthinking too many things, just racing off instincts. I think this is the perfect team for me to do that.”

The final frontier for American men’s cycling is on the horrendous cobblestones.

There’s room to write more history. The last top-10 by an American in the men’s Roubaix was Taylor Phinney with eighth in 2018, and Sheffield with sixth at Flanders in 2024.

Other U.S. riders, like Neilson Powless, Matteo Jorgenson, and Magnus Sheffield, have made some noise recently in the northern classics. Powless won Dwars door Vlaanderen in 2025 and was fifth at the 2023 Ronde, while Jorgenson won Dwars in 2024 and hit a top-10 at the Ronde in 2023.

Shmidt isn’t making any bold declarations about winning Flanders or Roubaix just yet.

For now, it’s about taking more chances and finding out what he can do when he’s off the leash.

title: Ducati's candidates to replace Marquez
author: Simon Patterson
text:
The shock news that Marc Marquez will call it quits on MotoGP at the end of this weekend creates a massive dilemma for Ducati, as it now tries to figure out exactly how to replace its star rider only days after he clinched another title success for the team and with 2027 testing about to begin.

Not since Jorge Lorenzo dramatically retired at the end of the 2019 season has a factory team had to find a new racer at the final round of the season, but it’s fair to say that the retirement of Marquez will create substantially more ripples through the grand prix paddock than his former rival’s did.

The most obvious solution, of course, is that Ducati promotes one of the rest of its line-up and, given the support and trust that Ducati Corse boss Gigi Dall’Igna has placed in since signing him as a then-rookie on a four-year MotoGP deal, it’s hard to imagine that it would be anyone else right now. That will create a vacancy at the VR46 team Aldeguer is currently scheduled to ride for next season.

Go beyond the headlines and sign up to The Lean Angle, The Race's MotoGP newsletter. You'll get bespoke content direct to your inbox every Tuesday, plus the occasional one-off edition like today, where we had a special on the Marquez retirement news .

The only other obvious contender is VR46's other 2027 signing: reigning World Superbike champion and 2027 MotoGP rookie - and the decision between which of the two is likely to get the nod will probably be measured in something that only Ducati has access to: lap times from testing on the 850cc bikes being used next year.

Aldeguer has already had a chance to jump onto next year’s factory bike, deputising for the departing Pecco Bagnaia at two post-race tests, but we’ve not heard much about how he performed in those closed-to-the-media outings at Brno and the Red Bull Ring.

However, while Aldeguer has had his time on the 850, Bulega has essentially been the lead development rider for the project thanks to his WSBK position meaning he’s not held back by MotoGP’s testing restrictions - and the initial suggestions have been that he has been very, very fast indeed.

Either way, though, the promotion of one of them to sit alongside Pedro Acosta in the most coveted seat in MotoGP will leave a space (ironically) at Valentino Rossi’s VR46 satellite team - a seat that might actually be harder to fill than Marquez’s.

The obvious choice, of course is Spanish Moto2 championship contender Manu Gonzalez, who goes into this weekend’s final race with a slender 4.5 point lead over already-confirmed 2027 MotoGP rookie Izan Guevara - and who many feel like has already been overlooked for a premier class seat for the past two seasons.

He already has limited MotoGP experience after standing in for Ai Ogura at Trackhouse Aprilia for a post-race test last year, and he certainly didn’t embarrass himself there. And while he’s already renewed with his IntactGP team for Moto2 next year, most contracts have a MotoGP escape clause - that is, after all, how Alex Marquez ended up joining his brother Marc at Repsol Honda in 2020, when he replaced Lorenzo.

One name that deserves to be in the conversation, of course, is this weekend's second factory Ducati rider , who has completed a number of very impressive MotoGP stand-in rides this year alongside his World Superbike duties.

However, he might have created a cross for his own back with a strong run of form as Bulega's number two this season, with Ducati's production bike hopes now resting firmly on his shoulders for 2027.

Of course, there’s an argument for helping one of the current MotoGP refugees find a spot for next year instead, with race winners such as and without a ride as things stand right now - but that will likely be a question decided on whether Ducati wants to invest in future potential, or is just looking for a one-year seat filler before is can settle things longer term during 2027.

That option might be interesting to the team, though, because it disrupts MotoGP’s two-year contract cycle a little - and potentially even opens the door to Marquez’s protege finding his way onto the MotoGP grid a little earlier than initially expected.

There’s a very short timeline on making those decisions, though, because Ducati will absolutely want its new rider, whoever it is, to make their debut for the factory next Tuesday at the post-race test, so that it can start the process of moulding them into a MotoGP racer sooner rather than later.

title: Our verdict on Marc Marquez's bombshell MotoGP retirement
author: The Race Team
text:
Marc Marquez dropped a huge bombshell as the final MotoGP round of the season kicked off at Valencia by announcing he is retiring from racing after this weekend.

Here's our take on the decision.

Who can blame him? Going out on top

There have been suggestions for weeks that Marc would retire at the end of the season, but it’s absolutely worth stressing this: almost none of them have come from inside the MotoGP paddock, with nearly everyone that you speak to (including people very much inside the Marquez inner circle) almost certain that he would continue on.

There was, so went the belief, still so much to come. New regulations for next year, and the chance to do what he’s never done and win on a different spec of bike. The opportunity to give us the moment Casey Stoner denied us, and test himself against his hotshot new Ducati team-mate Pedro Acosta.

Instead, he’s walked away - and honestly, after countless surgeries, dozens of broken bones, and 10 world titles, who can blame him? He’s going out on top, on his own terms.

What it says about his 2026 title

My apologies for bringing Formula 1 into this - I will keep it short. I remember being a fresh-faced editorial assistant when Nico Rosberg dropped his retirement announcement on us in 2016, and while those memories are so incredibly distinct (at home versus on track, new to the industry versus much more settled), the vision of it all is surprisingly similar.

When Rosberg got his one F1 title over the line, it was knife-edge. We all knew - he probably knew, too - that this was the one and only. He clearly accepted that quickly and was happy to leave it at that.

Marquez has won eight in MotoGP, but this is the first one he's won in this way. This is the first one that felt truly knife-edge, that felt lost and then found, that felt like it was taking more out of him than ever before and something different out of him than before.

He points-raced to it, with just a handful of crashes from his return at Mugello six months ago to now, whereas normally he was the one leading the crash standings. This time he played the odds and the opponent, and had to convince his body - the much-suffering arm, the diminished shoulder - to play along.

I have little doubt he could have won again. But I genuinely believe he no longer liked the odds, and could no longer justify to himself all the physical travails that would continue to be required to maintain those odds.

This adds to the legacy of his 2026 title, that I for so long didn't believe in. It was such a tightrope act that it's made the greatest rider in MotoGP history go 'OK, that was crazy - crazy enough to call it a day'.

Absolutely the right decision but a huge 2027 loss

Given everything his body has been through, everything he has achieved, this is absolutely the right moment for Marc Marquez to retire. He has nothing more to prove and there is no point risking yet more injuries. Totally, totally the right call.

But I am so, so, so gutted that we will now never get to see how him versus Acosta in the same team would have panned out.

Stoner's shock retirement months before Marquez arrived in MotoGP deprived us of one epic head to head, but was totally the right call for Stoner.

Now Marquez has deprived us of something that would have been even more epic.

But good for him. He's picked his moment perfectly.

The greatest I have ever seen

I'll keep it short and sweet: he has earned this moment. The amount of pain, suffering and ability to keep coming back again and again has finally taken its toll on him.

He retired on his terms, something that he may have thought might not have been possible just a few months ago with the state of his right arm. To win his 1oth world title through sheer mental strength and earn the right to be called the greatest motorcycle rider of all time is the perfect ending.

The greatest I have ever seen, what a pleasure it has been.

Stops any doubt about GOAT status

Marc Marquez's bombshell retirement will cement him as MotoGP's Greatest of All Time.

He was already that in my view - he's beaten many of MotoGP's other GOAT contenders to his first titles, and then won more after completing one of sport's great injury comebacks post-Jerez 2020 (and all the setbacks that followed).

But retiring now on his own terms ensures that nothing that happens in 2027 will change that.

Acosta was the only rider who I felt would have half a chance against Marquez on the same bike, and now Marquez won't be going head-to-head with him.

Had Marquez tripped up there - something not out of the question, given he'd have to adapt to a whole new formula and Acosta's enormous potential - that may have put an asterisk over his status as the GOAT.

Instead, Marquez has left the building and leaves behind a scrap to be MotoGP's new benchmark rider, a fight I wouldn't be surprised if his Ducati successor wins.

From a selfish point of view as an observer and fan of MotoGP, I don't want Marc to stop. But I get why it's happening. The mission is complete.

He's been through hell since 2020, fought back to the top of the mountain, got hurt a few more times along the way, and after dominating 2025 pulled off an unthinkable comeback in 2026.

What else is there left to achieve? How many more times should he risk destroying his body just because his presence in MotoGP is box office?

Of course I'd have loved to see him up against Acosta on equal machinery. But we'll just have to add that to the long list of epic head-to-heads we've narrowly missed out on in many forms of motorsport dating back decades.

Marquez has carried MotoGP on his shoulders for long enough. Those shoulders deserve a break, and now it's time for new stars to lead the series into its Liberty-owned era. Who's going to step up?

I expected to be making a coffee at the start of FP1, not watching the greatest MotoGP rider of all time announcing his retirement on some slides.

Taking a step back, this shouldn’t really be as shocking as it is, and yet we’re all speechless. This is a man whose body has been battered by countless injuries and surgeries over his career, but especially the last six years. This was a championship which came from 102 points back after yet more injury.

He’s now stepping away at the very top of his game, coming back from years of turmoil to reclaim his crown - not just once, but twice.

It is, of course, a shame that we won’t see Marquez vs Acosta, that much awaited battle between the king and the heir.

But whatever happens, it is beyond doubt now that Marc Marquez did it better than anyone else.

Blah blah blah, yeah yeah yeah… but ten.

He's never seemed so physically spent

Friday’s FP1 is usually a lower key ambience to kick off the weekend. But the eerie silence as the camera cut to Marc Marquez let us know something was up.

Ever the maestro of conducting the media off track, it was simple but utterly shocking to read the words 'This will be my last race in MotoGP'.

I expected a playful '…for 2026' to follow on a final card, but no. This is the end - mercifully, on track, on his own terms.

We will not see Marc on the next generation of MotoGP bikes. There will be no Honda reunion and no head to head with Pedro Acosta as Ducati’s newest prince in waiting.

There will not be an 11th world championship title. But for all the tantalising future narratives we lose, what an extraordinary chapter of MotoGP history we have witnessed.

The talent hasn’t diminished, the mind is sharper than ever, but the injuries have now clearly taken a toll too far to continue.

Reflecting on his 2026 season, Marc has never seemed so physically spent after his sessions, so there is a logic to this timing.

The 1000cc chapter closes, he has given everything, leaving this extraordinary sport battled-scarred but having made an impact as one of the true legends of motorcycle racing.

Someone give Gigi Dall’igna a hug, he’s had an emotional 24 hours.

Robs us of tantalising Acosta battle in 2027

In many ways, Marquez’s retirement makes sense: he arguably has nothing more to achieve, his body is already broken enough, and a retirement on his own terms is nothing less than he deserves.

I feel quite sentimental about the end of this chapter though. Hearing Marquez’s story about his attempted comeback in Jerez after that 2020 crash is what got me into MotoGP. Following along with his journey back from all of those injuries and struggles at Honda to his successes with Ducati has been incredible to watch.

He’s also cemented his status as the greatest of all time in my book, especially over the last two season. Could he have won again in 2027? I think so, but that’s something only he knows for sure.

So happy to have witnessed the (tail-end) of a stellar career and happy that he can end it this way. That being said, I’m slightly annoyed that we’ve been robbed of what could have been blockbuster battles between Marquez and Acosta at Ducati in 2027, and also extremely curious about what comes next.

I pity the first 'after-Marc' world champion

I sort of pity the first A.M. (after Marc) MotoGP world champion...

My main disappointment is we won't see if anyone could have properly overthrown him.

He'd so emphatically reminded everybody he was the best in the business that maybe he wouldn't have been beaten, of course.

It'll just feel slightly hollow for whoever succeeds him as world champion because justifiably or not there'll probably be that little asterisk of 'well, he only won because Marc stopped'.

I'm trying to consider a hypothetical F1 alternative that fits better than the obvious comparison of Nico Rosberg in 2016.

Rosberg was world champion but he wasn't the best driver in F1 at the time. So he couldn't be 'dethroned,' but I don't think there was an overarching 'ah, man, it would have been good to see who could have beat him' at play there.

With Marquez you know that MotoGP's losing the absolute benchmark.

title: My self-care ritual is a meal at a fancy restaurant - on my own
text:
Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat - bliss.

"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.

The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.

As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."

We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.

Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.

She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.

"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.

"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."

Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".

"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.

Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.

Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.

"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.

"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."

A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.

"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.

Ruth Alexander hears from solo diners - some who find peace and joy in a table for one, and others who would much rather not be alone

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".

But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.

"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."

SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners.

Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing."

However, some restaurants like Jungli, an Indian restaurant in Newcastle upon Tyne, is working to attract solo diners.

Co-founder and director Yousaf Khalid has included high tables and bar seats in his recently opened restaurant. They also have charging points for laptops and phones.

"We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.

He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience.

Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go.

"Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own.

"I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."

title: Pizza history: AI agent’s cardless purchase is a first for UK
author: Mark Sweney
text:
Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping

Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday

An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.

The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer.

“We completed this payment transaction with Papa John’s with no account numbers, no password [and] handled with the highest possible security profile,” said the TrueLayer chief executive, Francesco Simoneschi, in an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We talked with the AI agent, described the occasion and dietary requirements. Of course the agent suggested different flavours and quantities. We confirmed the order and the pizza arrived later.”

The team ordered the pizzas using the Papa John’s AI agent, which had been given permission to access their bank account and request payment to the retailer’s account.

Papa John’s AI agent was set to work with a strict mandate set with Lloyds, including a maximum spend limit per transaction and per month, with no account security information shared.

Simoneschi said the test was the first step toward mass adoption by the public of a technology that would fundamentally change purchasing habits.

“This is possibly the last Black Friday as we know it,” he said, referring to the annual online sales discount day. “At the moment plenty of us are already using AI to write up the shopping list. I think next year the agent will buy gifts on our behalf. Agents will do shopping on our behalf, will manage our finances, and will help us understand and compare complex products. This idea that they can really help us to sort out a lot of different aspects of our lives is a little bit like having an assistant available to millions of consumers out there.”

However, Simoneschi said consumers would still need to make informed decisions about how they used AI agents for making purchases.

“I think good [personal] judgment still applies, of course,” he said. “It does require control and supervision, and we need to make sure that the underlying technology is fit for purpose, while enforcing the highest possible security standards.”

He added that if there was an error or mistake in the order process, such as the agent ordering the wrong product, consumers would still be protected by existing rules and regulations covering buyers’ rights.

Earlier this week the FCA issued a warning to financial services companies developing AI agents that they must comply with existing regulations .

“The reason we are testing with regulators in this sandbox is to really understand all the aspects of the technology ahead of its mass adoption,” he said. “This is a great place to start.”

Meta’s personal AI assistant, Muse, which launched in the UK on Tuesday, can also make purchases online . Unlike TrueLayer, Muse makes payments using a customer’s bank card.

As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market . The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before.

title: ‘If the bot gets it wrong, who’s liable?’ Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday
author: Sarah Butler
text:
Brands know use of agents such as Meta Muse is on the rise but are unlikely to hand them the keys to the shop

Have you downloaded Meta’s AI assistant Muse or do you plan to?

They promise to find the best Black Friday deals, source Christmas gifts and find the ingredients for a romantic dinner.

This week’s UK launch of the Muse AI assistant by the owner of Facebook and Instagram promises to transform how we shop – and how retailers make money.

Meta has teamed up with high street names including Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury’s, JD Sports and Currys for what the Silicon Valley firm claims is a seamless, secure and time-saving tool.

“From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar … Muse can get it done for you,” Meta said.

But for companies that have painstakingly transformed from bricks-and-mortar retailers into online emporiums, AI agents pose risks as well as opportunities. Will AI agents kill window shopping, ignore vast online ranges and send shoppers straight to the checkout? Will retailers be forced to discount heavily to stand out? How do they avoid being steamrollered by Silicon Valley tech titans in commercial negotiations?

John Roberts, the founder and chief executive of online electrical goods retailer AO.com, said the impact of AI agents – at present – was “relatively low” but their use as shopping assistants was clearly “a direction of travel”.

He said AO was positioning itself to get recommendations from AI agents in the same way it generally attracted customers, by offering decent prices and good service, which was winning good online reviews on sites such as Trustpilot.

“We need to work out how we are the best option for whichever AI agent you use,” Roberts said.

Working out where to invest is a challenge. Some smaller firms are almost ignoring the developing channel, waiting to see how and where it might go. However, holding back on involvement with the developing technology – such as online shopping in the early noughties – has killed off brands in the past.

Sharon Iles, a senior apparel analyst at the analytics and consultancy firm GlobalData, said those brands that have chosen to partner with Muse would get an early view of how people shop, what they bought through an AI agent and which products got recommended, which could help brands make their listings more visible.

But she said retailers “must continue to prioritise their own channels to protect what an AI agent cannot replace”.

If agents bypass retailers’ websites, said Iles, this could mean companies “miss out on the impulse items that shoppers often add while browsing”, while those selling more complex items such as apparel could find issues with the choice of fit and sizing, “which could lead to higher return rates”.

“Retailers’ own channels should remain the core of their business, and they must give consumers more reasons to shop directly,” she said.

Retailers including Sainsbury’s and Tesco have used their loyalty schemes and websites to build sizeable businesses that monetise customers’ data and sell advertising space to brands.

However, retailers cannot ignore the agents. Muse has proved successful in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, having been downloaded millions of times.

UK residents may be more cautious about agentic technology than those across the Atlantic, but the technology is entering the mainstream. This year, a third of people planning to shop during Black Friday sales intend to get help from AI – up from 19% last year, according to a recent YouGov poll.

To fans, the likes of Muse or rivals such as Google’s Gemini or ChatGPT’s Dots can be a personal secretary helping organise the boring details of life, but to others they are an untenable busybody, parsing their personal data and monetising it.

For Muse to work as Meta envisages, it not only needs access to your email, calendar and shopping apps but details of relationships on apps such as WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, your preferences and even your financial and health information.

Sainsbury’s suggests its customers can “tell Muse about their week” and the AI agent will help build a shopping list to provide for dinner parties, different dietary requirements or suggest menus and recipes.

Mark Given, the chief technology and marketing officer at the supermarket chain, said the retailer was “starting carefully, listening to customers” and using what we learn to keep making it better”.

“AI can be genuinely useful, taking on routine tasks like checking offers and building the basket, and helping customers find great value and inspiration more quickly,” he said.

In the UK, Muse must ask for your approval before making a purchase or sending an email, while a separate “security agent” checks the AI tool’s actions against the permissions you have granted.

Meta said Muse had no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods, and it did not share users’ conversations with advertisers.

However, almost half of shoppers using AI (48%) are concerned about biased or sponsored recommendations, according to YouGov. Rival research firm Kantar found only 23% trusted a chatbot’s recommendations.

Meanwhile, some retailers are territorial about which AI agents get to trawl their data. Amazon has blocked AI agents from its store, although it is reportedly in talks with Meta about allowing access. Last year, Amazon sued the AI company Perplexity over its shopping feature that automates placing orders for users.

Research from the advisory firm KPMG highlights consumer caution. It found just 12% of those planning to shop during Black Friday – a largely online sale event in the UK – intended to use an AI tool (such as prompting ChatGPT or Gemini) specifically to find deals, slightly lower than the 15% using it last year.…

title: The food bank helping pet owners with rising bills
text:
At Burngreave Foodbank in Sheffield, a queue of worried people are here not to collect groceries for themselves, but food for their pets.

The RSPCA has launched a pop-up food bank to hand out cat litter, veterinary vouchers and pet toys as well as food.

Many of the dog and cat owners using the service say that rising bills are leaving them in fear they will not be able to care for their beloved companions.

John Paul Feely, 59, has four cats and a dog, and currently spends £35 a month on them.

"At the moment we're facing rises in fuel costs, food costs and you've got to make a choice at some point, can we look after the animals?" he says.

Feely worries that unexpected vet bills as well as the day-to-day expenses could tip him over the edge when his energy bill goes up in January.

Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year.

The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.

Feely lives with his partner and explains that they are already making tough decisions about "turning the lights out and not putting the heating on".

He is able to take home food supplies and a dog chew toy.

As food bank volunteers offer tea and coffee to those waiting in the queue, Angela Gillot accepts a small dog jacket from the RSPCA stall with a smile.

She explains with a tear in her eye that since becoming unemployed she has felt the pinch of rising bills.

The RSPCA estimates that the cost of keeping a small dog like a Jack Russell could be up to £209 a month.

Energy costs going up next year "will affect everything," Gillot admits, as she describes how she and her dog huddle up under a blanket to keep warm.

"We do love these pets. We're a pet-loving nation aren't we? But it's getting harder.

"When I got my dogs I was working, so I try my best, but the price of food, especially what's of quality, I just really can't afford it.

"It's not often you go to these places and they think about your pets," the 58-year-old says.

Tricia Watts, the upbeat assistant manger at Burngreave Foodbank, is enthusiastic about the support from the RSPCA.

She explains that while the food bank works with people in food poverty, it cannot always help people with animal care as it relies on donations.

She has seen demand increase, and donations fall, in the seven years she has worked at the food bank.

"I think pets are so important to people. If people are going through hard times, they're still important and they don't want to lose them."

Growing bills are of particular concern to exotic animal owners as many birds, reptiles and fish must be kept in carefully maintained conditions that are often energy-intensive.

Carl Chandler runs Sustainable Aquatics in Rotherham. He says rising energy prices have had a "gigantic" impact on his business.

Chandler caveats that fish are one of the most wallet-friendly pets.

"To run a tropical fish tank you're looking less than a cup of coffee a week."

Other species, however, require specialist equipment to replicate their natural habitats.

"Reptiles, frogs and amphibians are incredibly expensive to heat because you need UV bulbs and to keep the right humidity."

Back in Burngreave, the pop-up event has managed to give away as much as 50kg of food, the equivalent of more than 100 tins, to pet owners in need.

Sometimes, of course, owners find the challenge simply too much, and give their pets up for rehoming.

"We've seen heartbreaking examples across the country of people leaving notes with animals saying they just can't afford them any more," Chris O'Brien, a spokesperson for the RSPCA, says.

"The cost of giving crisis has put new levels of pressure on us in terms of animals coming in quicker than we can rehome them.

"As these cost of living bombshells keep coming, unfortunately it's going to be a continued difficult time for animal owners across the region."

title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
author: Eromo Egbejule in Lagos
text:
What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape

A s a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.

“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara , meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.

“We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

T he hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.

Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.

Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.

“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

D espite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.

“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

Back in the 1990s, one way to preserve basketball games for the future was to record them on a VHS cassette. For all the younger folks, this was a big, chunky, rectangular thing that had magnetic tape on the inside. Whenever a game was on TV, you popped your cassette into the video recorder, pressed “REC,” and from that point on, you could rewatch anything you recorded whenever you wanted. Or for as long as the tape held up, for that matter.

My favorite recorded event back then was Game Five of the first round of the playoffs in 1999 between your New York Knicks and the Miami Heat. It ended with Allan Houston’s historic leaning jumper with 0.8 seconds to go, sending the top-seeded team coached by the Godfather of Schenectady packing and the underdog Bockers on an improbable run all the way to the NBA Finals. The tape wasn’t just special to me because of the historic shot or the basketball played with bad intentions back then. It was also awesome because it showed the Knicks beating the Heat. Sorry, Grandma, I know you taught me not to hate anyone, but those were the Heat, my favorite team’s biggest rival for years.

Now, before A’ja Wilson’s boyfriend thinks he can hold a candle to the guy Patrick Ewing once offered one of his kidneys to, let me make it clear: That was a different time, a different rivalry. Whoever experienced it firsthand knows what I mean by that. When the Knicks meet the Heat on Friday night for their fourth NBA Cup game of the season, it will be different, much different. Different players, different coaches. Heck, it all seems like a different world. But make no mistake about it—it’s still Knicks versus Heat. Which means the stakes are just a bit higher than in a game versus the magicians from the nation’s capital or the royalty from “The Big Tomato.”

Knicks get first look at Giannis on the Heat

Friday’s game will be particularly interesting because it gives the Knicks a first glimpse at the newest version of the Heat, featuring Greece’s national hero Giannis Antetokounmpo, who also happens to be one of the greatest and probably most unique basketball players this generation has seen. The project started pretty badly, with Giannis continuously reminding everyone who cared and everyone who didn’t that he dearly missed Milwaukee, the city he had called home for every second of his storied NBA career until then. Then the schematic issues befell the not-so-hot Heat, who struggled with spacing, players playing in new roles, and the daunting task of implementing a headstrong player with immense gravity into a completely new system. Defense? Haha, good one!

But after a 3-6 start, the second-oldest team in the league decided this wasn’t the way to ride off into the sunset. Or rather, their famous coach made plenty of adjustments. Erik Spoelstra, as we all know, is one of the best in the business. Not only at taking average rosters into the Play-In Tournament but indeed at coaching that sport with the orange leather. He inserted young Pelle Larsson into the starting lineup, found a spacing solution for the Heat, doubled down on their identity as a full-court, offensive-minded team, and then watched his guys reel off seven mostly impressive victories in a row (among them wins over Houston and Detroit) before falling to Philly on Wednesday night.

What can we expect from the Heat specifically? They love to get up and down the court and play at the third-highest pace in the entire league. Currently, only the Memphis Grizzlies score more points than Spoelstra’s squad, and the Heat do it by shooting a high percentage from the field, drawing boatloads of fouls, and making use of two post players. Yes, you read that right—post players. Both Giannis and A’ja Wilson’s boyfriend can effectively score with their backs to the basket, and despite many worries, they can actually coexist next to one another. One of them fills the dunker spot almost all the time, they rotate decisively in screen actions, and overall, Miami runs its sets fast and ferociously to get them rolling downhill. They don’t just set screens to see where it leads them; they want to get into an action quickly before any lanes can close.

Heat, Spoelstra have adjusted after bad start

It works, partly because the players around Giannis and that guy who made a habit last year of disliking the team that won a championship before him are all doing a good job in their roles. Klay Thompson adds shooting (43.2 percent from downtown), Swedish Swiss Army knife Pelle Larsson provides a little bit of everything, and playmaker Davion Mitchell has all of a sudden turned into one of the better point guards in the league at age 28, averaging career highs of 17 points and 8.6 assists per contest while also shooting 51 percent from the floor and 43-plus percent from behind the arc. The bench has some older vets more or less collecting paychecks so far, but Bobby Portis and Andrew Wiggins clearly have some talent. Apparently, that also describes Ryan Conwell, a stocky second-round guard who has been a pleasant surprise for Miami.

That whole group will definitely look to waltz into Madison Square Garden on Friday with the idea of showing the champs that they are a team to be reckoned with. Whether they truly are remains to be seen; there are plenty of things that could uproot the positivity currently sprawling across South Beach. But the Knicks better be prepared for a tough test, and not because they might still be missing some of their injured guys or because they are coming off an emotionally draining victory against Cleveland on Wednesday. Not even because A’ja Wilson might have taught her boyfriend a few more tricks this offseason after winning her fifth WNBA MVP trophy.

No, it’s going to be tough because it’s Heat versus Knicks. And even if that doesn’t mean what it did in the days of the VHS cassette, it still means something.

title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
text:
Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election

The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.

The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.

The National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will likely need to hold another election.

Three electorate seats changed hands following the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from of National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.

If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.

Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.

After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.

On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.

“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”

Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong , has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.

After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.

The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.

“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.

Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.

“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”

Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision . Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.

Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.

“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.

In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.

New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.
